title: HTTP Caching
summary: This document defines HTTP caches and the header fields that control cache behavior or mark responses as cacheable. It is part of the revised HTTP specification and obsoletes RFC 7234.

eli5.summary: A cache keeps a copy of something you got so next time you get it faster. This document explains the rules about when websites let copies be kept and reused.

questions: what is the difference between no-cache and no-store
how does http cache validation work
subtitle: The rules for when HTTP responses may be stored, reused, checked again and thrown away.

tldr.problem: Fetching the same response again and again from an origin server wastes time and bandwidth, but reusing a stored copy carelessly can serve wrong or private data.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9111 defines when a cache may store a response, how it decides the copy is still fresh, how it validates a stale copy with a conditional request, and which header fields (Cache-Control, Age, Expires) steer all of that.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 7234, and it deprecates Pragma and obsoletes Warning.

today: RFC 9111 is an Internet Standard (STD 98) and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 7234, and the semantics it relies on are defined in RFC 9110.

sections.title: What an HTTP Cache Is
sections.content:
An HTTP cache is a local store of response messages plus the subsystem that controls storage, retrieval and deletion. It stores cacheable responses to reduce response time and network bandwidth on future equivalent requests. Any client or server MAY use a cache, though not when acting as a tunnel.

A shared cache stores responses for reuse by more than one user and is usually part of an intermediary. A private cache is dedicated to a single user and is often a component of a user agent.

The goal is to reuse a prior response to satisfy a current request. A stored response is fresh if it can be reused without validation, which means checking with the origin server that it is still valid. A stale response might still be reusable if validation can freshen it or if the origin is unavailable. The document obsoletes RFC 7234.
sections.eli5: A cache is like keeping a copy of a library book at home. You do not walk to the library each time, but you need rules for when your copy is too old to trust.

sections.title: Overview of Cache Operation
sections.content:
Caching is an entirely OPTIONAL feature of HTTP. Reuse is assumed to be desirable and is the default when no requirement or local configuration prevents it, so the rules mostly stop a cache from storing a non-reusable response or reusing a stored one inappropriately.

The cache key is the information a cache uses to choose a response. At a minimum it is the request method and target URI. Many caches only store GET responses and so use just the URI. When a resource uses content negotiation, the Vary response header field adds request header fields to the key. Caches may add more, for example the referring site's identity, which is called double keying.

Most often a cache stores a 200 (OK) response to a GET. It may also store redirects, negative results such as 404, incomplete results such as 206, and responses to other methods if the method's definition allows it. A cache is disconnected when it cannot contact the origin server.
sections.eli5: The cache needs a label for each saved copy, like writing the web address on a lunchbox. If the same address can have different versions, the label also says which version it is.

sections.title: Storing and Reusing Responses
sections.content:
A cache MUST NOT store a response unless a list of conditions holds. Among them: it understands the request method, the status code is final, the response has no no-store directive, and a shared cache sees no private directive and no Authorization request header unless a directive explicitly allows sharing. The response must also carry something that makes it cacheable, such as public, max-age, Expires, s-maxage (for shared caches), or a status code defined as heuristically cacheable.

Caches MUST keep all received response header fields, including unrecognized ones, so new fields can be deployed, with exceptions such as Connection and proxy-specific fields. Trailer fields may be stored separately or discarded, but MUST NOT be combined with header fields. Partial content may be stored and later combined only if the ranges share the same strong validator.

To reuse a stored response the target URI must match, the stored request method must allow it, request fields named by Vary must match, any no-cache must have been satisfied by validation, and the response must be fresh, allowed to be served stale, or successfully validated. A reused response without validation gets an Age header field. Unsafe methods must be written through to the origin, and with several matches the most recent one (by Date) MUST be used. A Vary field containing the wildcard member always fails to match.
sections.eli5: Before keeping a copy, the cache checks a list of do-not-keep signs, like a note saying private. Before handing a copy out, it checks it is the right one and not too old.

sections.title: Freshness and Age
sections.content:
A response is fresh while its age has not exceeded its freshness lifetime, and stale once it has. The test is response_is_fresh = (freshness_lifetime > current_age).

The freshness lifetime is taken from the first rule that matches: s-maxage for a shared cache, then max-age, then Expires minus Date. If none is present, a cache MAY assign a heuristic lifetime, but only for status codes defined as heuristically cacheable or responses marked explicitly cacheable, and never when an explicit time exists. Where Last-Modified is present, caches are encouraged to use no more than some fraction of the time since then, and a typical fraction might be 10%.

Age is estimated from the Age header, the Date header and the cache's own clock, plus time spent resident in the cache. Duplicate or conflicting directives should lead to the first value being used or the response being treated as stale, and the most restrictive directive should be honored. Invalid freshness information, such as a non-integer max-age, should be treated as stale. A cache MUST NOT generate a stale response if a directive such as no-cache or must-revalidate forbids it, and otherwise only when disconnected or explicitly permitted. A cache without a clock MUST revalidate on every use.
sections.eli5: Milk has a use-by date. While it is before that date you can use it freely. After it, you check with the shop first, unless the shop said it is fine to use it a bit late.

sections.title: Validation and Invalidation
sections.content:
When a cache has a stored response it cannot serve as is, it can send a conditional request to ask whether its copy is still good. It adds validators from the stored response: entity tags go in If-None-Match (and the cache MUST send them if provided), and a Last-Modified value goes in If-Modified-Since (which it SHOULD send). Usually both are sent, so old intermediaries that do not understand entity tags still respond appropriately.

A 304 (Not Modified) response means the stored response can be updated and reused. The cache picks which stored responses to update by strong validators first, then weak validators, then the case where no validators exist. A full response replaces the stored one, and a 5xx may be forwarded or treated as if the server did not answer. A cache can also use a HEAD response to update or invalidate stored GET responses.

Unsafe methods such as PUT, POST or DELETE change state, so a cache MUST invalidate the target URI when it sees a non-error (2xx or 3xx) response to one. It MAY invalidate URIs in Location and Content-Location, but MUST NOT do so when their origin differs from the target's, which helps prevent denial-of-service attacks.
sections.eli5: When the milk is past its date, you phone the shop and ask whether it is still good. If the shop says yes, you keep using it and write down a new date. If someone changes the recipe, you throw the old copy away.

sections.title: Cache-Control and the Other Fields
sections.content:
The Cache-Control header field lists directives for caches along the request and response chain. Directives are unidirectional, a proxy MUST pass them through even if it has no cache, and a cache MUST ignore unrecognized ones. Request directives are advisory. Response directives MUST be obeyed.

  • max-age: stale after this many seconds. s-maxage overrides it for shared caches and implies proxy-revalidate.
  • no-cache: the response must be validated before every reuse.
  • no-store: do not store any part of the request or response. The RFC says this is not a reliable privacy mechanism.
  • private: a shared cache MUST NOT store it. public explicitly marks a response as cacheable.
  • must-revalidate: once stale, never reuse without successful validation, even when disconnected, in which case an error such as 504 is generated.
  • must-understand: only cache if the status code's caching rules are understood.
  • Request side: max-stale, min-fresh and only-if-cached.

The Age field carries the estimated seconds since generation or validation. Expires gives an absolute date, invalid dates such as 0 mean already expired, and it is ignored when max-age is present. Pragma is deprecated and Warning is obsoleted. Values of delta-seconds beyond what a cache can represent are treated as 2147483648 (2^31).
sections.eli5: Cache-Control is a set of sticky notes the server puts on a response. One says keep for ten minutes, another says do not keep, another says only the owner may keep it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Cache contents persist after a request completes, so an attack on the cache can reveal information long after a user believes it is gone. Cache contents need protecting as sensitive information, and users should be able to control private caches, for example by removing stored responses for some or all origin servers.

Cache poisoning means inserting a malicious response into a cache, which is especially effective on shared caches that serve many clients. One common vector is differences in message parsing between proxies and user agents.

Timing attacks work because a fast load reveals that a resource was fetched earlier. Adding the referring site to the cache key (double keying) mitigates this. Finally, caching can expose sensitive information through misunderstanding: Set-Cookie does not inhibit caching, so servers should emit appropriate Cache-Control fields.
sections.eli5: A cache is a drawer full of copies, so a thief or a sneaky site might learn what you looked at. The rules say to guard the drawer and to label private things so they are not shared.
